title: Non-Iterative Electron Ptychography With Relaxed Real-Space Sampling
content: The development of electron ptychography has enabled unprecedented improvements in resolution, light-element sensitivity and sample thickness limits for scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). By acquiring a two-dimensional array of two-dimensional diffraction patterns and implementing phase retrieval algorithms, the complex object (i.e. the sample) and probe can be reconstructed with high fidelity and sensitivity. While initial demonstrations of STEM ptychography were performed using direct, non-iterative phase retrieval methods such as Wigner distribution deconvolution (WDD) [1,2] and single side band (SSB) methods [3], their strict sampling limitations have led to them being replaced by modern iterative algorithms. This is because both SSB and WDD typically involve a data reduction step, in which the processed data is compressed from 4D to 2D, where the remaining two-dimensions correspond to the scan array. Only one complex pixel is typically reconstructed for each scan position, and thus the scanning step size must be sufficiently small to sample high-resolution features in the reconstruction. This problem is compounded by slow readout speeds of commercial detectors, such that a 10nm x 10nm array of diffraction patterns may take several minutes to acquire. In contrast, modern electron ptychography methods involve robust iterative procedures which utilize sampling in the detector plane, such that large fields of view can be scanned with large step sizes [4,5]. While these algorithms are powerful, they are highly parametrized and must converge upon successive iterations to generate a faithful result. Recently, there has been increasing interest in relaxing the sampling constraints of non-iterative ptychography to enable robust and straightforward STEM phase imaging [6].
